jingyesi.summary: A five-character quatrain. On an autumn night far from home, the poet sees moonlight by his bed and takes it for frost on the ground; he looks up at the moon, then bows his head in longing for home. The language is plain and the mood cool and still.
jingyesi.translation:
Bright moonlight before my bed,
I wonder if it is frost on the ground.
I lift my head and gaze at the bright moon,
I lower it and think of my old home.

glossary.note: Most editions print the common form 「床」; it means a piece of furniture for sitting or lying on. One reading takes it as the railing around a well.
Here the poet mistakes the moonlight for frost.
To lift one's head.
One's home town or home region.

jingyesi.background: By Li Bai, the great Tang dynasty (618-907) poet. It is usually thought to date from a stay in Yangzhou, far from home. It is one of the most widely known short poems in Chinese.

chunxiao.summary: A five-character quatrain. The poet wakes on a spring morning to birdsong all around, recalls the wind and rain of the night, and wonders how many blossoms have fallen. The words are simple, and they carry a quiet affection for spring and a faint regret.
chunxiao.translation:
Sleeping in spring, I do not notice the dawn,
On every side I hear the birds singing.
There was the sound of wind and rain in the night,
How many flowers have fallen, who knows.

glossary.note: Spring nights are short and the sleep is sweet.

glossary.en: bu jue xiao - 'not noticing the dawn'
glossary.note: It is light before one realises.
Birds that are calling out.

glossary.en: zhi duo shao - 'who knows how many'
glossary.note: Meaning 'there is no knowing how many'.

chunxiao.background: By Meng Haoran, a High Tang poet of landscapes and rural life, who lived for many years in retirement on Deer Gate Mountain near Xiangyang. The poem describes a spring morning in that quiet life.

dengguanquelou.summary: A five-character quatrain. The first two lines describe the view from the tower: the sun setting behind the hills and the Yellow River flowing into the sea. The last two draw a lesson from the scene: to see farther, climb one more storey. It is a famous image of aspiration.
dengguanquelou.translation:
The white sun sinks along the hills,
The Yellow River flows into the sea.
To see a thousand li to the end,
Climb one more storey higher.

glossary.note: A tower in present-day Yongji, Shanxi, beside the Yellow River. It was named for the storks (guanque) that often perched there.

glossary.en: jin - 'to be used up, to vanish'
glossary.note: To sink out of sight, to be gone.
To reach the very limit of something.
A view that reaches a thousand li (about 500 km) into the distance.

dengguanquelou.background: Wang Zhihuan was a High Tang poet known for frontier verse. The Stork Tower stood at Puzhou (now Yongji, Shanxi) and looked down on the Yellow River. The poem has only twenty characters but a wide view, and its last line has become a set phrase.

xiangsi.summary: A five-character quatrain. Red beans growing in the south stand for longing: the poet urges a friend to gather many, because nothing else speaks so well of missing someone. The language is plain and the feeling deep.
xiangsi.translation:
Red beans grow in the southern lands,
How many new shoots come with spring.
I hope you will gather plenty of them,
For nothing else so brings to mind the longing of friends.

glossary.note: Also called 'seeds of longing' (xiangsizi). The beans are bright red, and in old China they stood for missing someone.
The south.
To pick. The second character is read xie.

glossary.en: xiang si - 'to long for each other'
glossary.note: To think of one another.

xiangsi.background: By Wang Wei. The poem is also known under the title 'Presented to Li Guinian by the River', and some read it as written for a friend far away. The red bean is a common image of longing in Tang poetry.

luzhai.summary: A five-character quatrain. In an empty mountain the poet sees no one, only hears voices far off; then the slanting evening light enters the deep wood and falls on the moss. Sound makes the stillness deeper, and the poem has a Chan (Zen) calm.
luzhai.translation:
In the empty mountain I see no one,
I only hear the echo of voices.
The returning light enters the deep wood,
And shines again on the green moss.

glossary.note: A place name: one of the scenic spots of Wang Wei's country estate at Wangchuan. The second character is read zhai and here stands for 'stockade'.
Simply, only.
The light of the setting sun shining back across the land. The second character is an old way of writing 'shadow' or 'light'.
Once more.

luzhai.background: Wang Wei spent his later years in retirement at Wangchuan and wrote twenty poems for the Wangchuan Collection; this is one of them. Wang Wei was both poet and painter, and this poem has the look of a painting and the feeling of Chan Buddhism.

zhuliguan.summary: A five-character quatrain. The poet sits alone in a quiet bamboo grove, plays the zither and whistles long; no one knows he is there, and only the bright moon comes to keep him company. It shows the peace and contentment of a life in retirement.
zhuliguan.translation:
Sitting alone in the shade of the bamboo,
I play the zither and whistle long.
In the deep wood no one knows I am here,
Only the bright moon comes to shine on me.

glossary.note: One of the spots at the Wangchuan estate, set among bamboo.
A deep, quiet bamboo grove. The second character means a bamboo grove.
Pursing the lips to make a long, clear sound. Scholars of the time used it to give vent to their feelings.

glossary.en: xiang zhao - 'to shine on one another'
glossary.note: To light each other up.

zhuliguan.background: By Wang Wei, from the Wangchuan Collection. The poem expresses the calm, undemanding mind of a man living in retirement.

jiangxue.summary: A five-character quatrain. Against a world made utterly still, with no birds in the hills and no footprints on the paths, one old man in a straw cape and hat fishes alone on a snowy river. The poem is lofty and lonely, and it hints at the poet's own proud isolation in exile.
jiangxue.translation:
On a thousand hills the birds have stopped flying,
On ten thousand paths no footprint is left.
In a lone boat, an old man in a straw cape and hat
Fishes by himself in the cold river snow.

glossary.en: jue - 'to cut off, to be none'
glossary.note: To be gone entirely.
Footprints of people.

glossary.en: suo li - 'straw cape and bamboo hat'
glossary.note: Rain gear worn in wet or snowy weather. The first character is read suo.
The chilly water of a river in winter.

jiangxue.background: Liu Zongyuan wrote this while demoted to Yongzhou (in present-day Hunan). The lonely fisherman can be read as a picture of the poet himself: aloof, upright and alone.

youziyin.summary: A five-character poem in the old style. It begins with a small detail, a mother sewing clothes for a son about to travel, and goes on to the gratitude children feel for a mother's love. The last two lines compare a child's small devotion to an inch of grass and a mother's love to the sun of spring, a debt too great to repay.
youziyin.translation:
In a loving mother's hands, needle and thread;
On the body of a wandering son, a coat.
As he leaves, she sews it close, stitch on stitch,
Fearing he will be slow to come home.
Who says the heart of a blade of grass
Can repay the warmth of the spring sun?

glossary.note: Someone who has left home and is living away.
To worry that.

glossary.en: cun cao xin - 'the heart of an inch of grass'
glossary.note: The heart of a little blade of grass: an image of the small devotion a child can offer.

glossary.en: san chun hui - 'the sunshine of the three months of spring'
glossary.note: The sunlight of spring, standing for a mother's love. 'Three springs' means the first, middle and last months of the season.

youziyin.background: By Meng Jiao, a Tang dynasty (618-907) poet. A note he added to the poem says it was written when he welcomed his mother to his post. Meng Jiao was past fifty before he took a minor office at Liyang, and he brought his mother to live with him there.

susdejiang.summary: A five-character quatrain. The poet moors his boat by a misty river bank at dusk, and the sorrow of being far from home comes over him again. The fields are wide, the sky seems to hang low over the trees, the river is clear and the moon seems close: the scene answers the feeling.
susdejiang.translation:
I move the boat and moor by a misty islet,
At sunset the traveller's sorrow comes fresh.
The plain is vast, the sky hangs low over the trees,
The river is clear, the moon comes close to me.

glossary.en: Jiande Jiang - 'the Jiande stretch of the river'
glossary.note: The part of the Xin'an River that flows past Jiande county.
A small sandbank or islet wrapped in mist. The second character is read zhu.

glossary.en: ke chou xin - 'the traveller's sorrow is new'
glossary.note: The sorrow of the traveller comes again, as if new.

glossary.en: ye kuang tian di shu - 'the plain is wide, the sky low over the trees'
glossary.note: The open land stretches far and the sky seems to sink to the tops of the trees.

susdejiang.background: Meng Haoran travelled in the regions of Wu and Yue (the lower Yangtze area) in his prime, and this poem was written on the way. His feelings as a traveller, after failing the civil service examinations, blend with the dusk on the river.

xunyinzhe.summary: A five-character quatrain written as a question and answer. The poet goes to visit a hermit and does not find him; through the boy's reply we see a hermit who comes and goes unseen, lofty and apart from the world.
xunyinzhe.translation:
Beneath the pines I ask a boy,
He says his master has gone to gather herbs.
He is somewhere in this very mountain,
But the clouds are deep and I cannot say where.

glossary.note: A person of high character who lives in retirement.
A young attendant.
Hermits often earned a living by gathering medicinal herbs.

glossary.en: yun shen bu zhi chu - 'the clouds are deep, I do not know where'
glossary.note: The clouds are so thick that it is impossible to tell where he is.

xunyinzhe.background: By Jia Dao, a poet of the 'painful chanting' school, who laboured over every word. He is best known for the story of 「推敲」 ('push or knock'), about choosing a single word. This poem is written entirely as dialogue; it is short and leaves much unsaid.

wenliushijiu.summary: A five-character quatrain in which the poet invites his friend Liu Shijiu for a drink. New wine, a small red clay stove and an evening that looks like snow make a warm picture. The words are plain and the feeling is deep.
wenliushijiu.translation:
New wine, unstrained, with green froth like ants,
A little stove of red clay.
As evening comes, the sky is about to snow,
Can you take a cup with me, or not?

glossary.note: The green froth floating on new wine, which looks like tiny ants. The second character is an old form of the character for 'ant'.
Wine that has not yet been filtered. It is read pei.

glossary.en: hong ni xiao huo lu - 'small stove of red clay'
glossary.note: A little stove fired from red clay.
A question word at the end of a sentence, equal to 'or not'.

wenliushijiu.background: By Bai Juyi. Liu Shijiu ('Liu, the nineteenth' in his family) was a friend of his from the time he was posted at Jiangzhou (now Jiujiang, Jiangxi). The poem has only twenty characters, but it shows the warmth of friendship in simple language.

dengleyouyuan.summary: A five-character quatrain. Uneasy at dusk, the poet drives up to an ancient plain; the setting sun is beautiful, but it is already close to nightfall. The poem holds a feeling about passing time and about his own situation.
dengleyouyuan.translation:
Towards evening my mind was not at ease,
I drove my carriage up the ancient plain.
The setting sun is beautiful beyond measure,
It is only that dusk is near.

glossary.note: A high piece of ground south of the Tang capital, Chang'an, and a favourite place for outings.
As evening approaches.

glossary.en: yi bu shi - 'the mind not at ease'
glossary.note: Feeling unsettled or low.
So beautiful that it cannot be measured.

dengleyouyuan.background: By Li Shangyin. The line 「夕陽無限好，只是近黃昏」 can be read as admiration of the view, or as a sigh over a declining age, or over the poet's own late years.

zaofabaidi.summary: A seven-character quatrain. Pardoned on his way into exile, the poet sails east down the Yangtze and reaches Jiangling in a single day from Baidi City. The rhythm is light and the mountains and water rush by, showing the relief and joy of a man set free.
zaofabaidi.translation:
At dawn I leave Baidi, among the coloured clouds,
A thousand li to Jiangling, back in a single day.
On both banks the monkeys' cries have not ceased,
When the light boat has already passed ten thousand hills.

glossary.note: A town in present-day Fengjie, Chongqing, at the western entrance to the Three Gorges of the Yangtze.
Today's Jingzhou in Hubei.
To go back, or to get there.

glossary.en: wan chong shan - 'ten thousand folds of hills'
glossary.note: Hills in layer upon layer: the mountains of the Three Gorges.

zaofabaidi.background: In 759, the second year of the Qianyuan era under Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty (618-907), Li Bai was exiled to Yelang because of the affair of Prince Yong, Li Lin. He was pardoned when he reached Baidi City, and wrote this poem as he sailed downstream.

fengqiaoyebo.summary: A seven-character quatrain. The poet moors at Maple Bridge at night: the moon has set, a crow calls, frost fills the sky, and he cannot sleep for sorrow, facing the river maples and the fishing lights. At midnight the bell of Cold Mountain Temple reaches his boat. The scene is finely drawn, and a traveller's sadness is woven into the cold night.
fengqiaoyebo.translation:
The moon sets, crows call, frost fills the sky,
River maples and fishing fires face me in my sorrowful sleeplessness.
Outside Gusu city, at Cold Mountain Temple,
The midnight bell reaches the traveller's boat.

glossary.note: A bridge outside the Chang Gate of Suzhou. It was originally called Feng Qiao, 'Sealed Bridge', written with a different character.
The cawing of crows. One reading takes the two characters as a place name.
He lies facing his sorrow. Another reading takes 'Chou Mian' as the name of a hill by the river.

glossary.en: ye ban zhong sheng - 'the midnight bell'
glossary.note: In the Song dynasty (960-1279) Ouyang Xiu doubted that temples rang bells at midnight, but a midnight bell is found often in Tang poems.

fengqiaoyebo.background: By Zhang Ji, said to have been written when he passed through Suzhou after the An Lushan rebellion. The poem made Maple Bridge and Cold Mountain Temple famous throughout China.

liangzhouci.summary: A seven-character quatrain. Soldiers on a frontier campaign drink at a feast: fine wine in a night-glowing cup, a lute urging them on as they drink deep. It seems bold, but beneath it lies the sadness of men who do not know whether they will live.
liangzhouci.translation:
Grape wine in cups that glow at night,
I mean to drink, and the pipa on horseback urges me on.
If I lie drunk on the battlefield, do not laugh at me,
From of old, how many have come back from war?

glossary.note: The name of a Tang folk-song tune (yuefu). Liangzhou is in present-day Wuwei, Gansu.
A cup said to be made of fine jade that shines at night.

glossary.en: pipa ma shang cui - 'the pipa urges from horseback'
glossary.note: One reading is that mounted soldiers play the pipa (a plucked lute) to urge others to drink.
A field of battle.

liangzhouci.background: Wang Han was a High Tang poet of a free and bold character. The poem is about drinking and merrymaking, but its last line, 「古來征戰幾人回」 ('how many have returned from war since ancient times'), speaks of the cruelty of war.

chusai.summary: A seven-character quatrain. The poet begins with the long history of unrest on the frontier since the Qin and Han dynasties, laments the endless wars and the soldiers who never come home, and hopes for a commander like Li Guang to guard the border so that enemy horsemen dare not come south.
chusai.translation:
The moon is that of Qin times, the pass that of Han times,
Men who marched ten thousand li have not yet returned.
If only the Flying General of Dragon City were here,
He would not let the Hu horses cross the Yin Mountains.

glossary.en: Chu sai - 'Going Out to the Frontier'
glossary.note: The name of a Tang dynasty (618-907) folk-song tune (yuefu), one of the 'horseback songs' of the frontier.
One reading takes it as the place where the Xiongnu, the nomadic enemies of Han China, worshipped Heaven; another reads it as the Dragon City that the general Wei Qing attacked.
Li Guang, a famous general of the Western Han dynasty (206 BC-9 AD), whom the Xiongnu called the 'Flying General'.
A range in present-day Inner Mongolia, which since the Han has served as a barrier against the Xiongnu.

chusai.background: Wang Changling was a High Tang poet of frontier verse and a master of the seven-character quatrain. Ming critics ranked this poem among the best Tang quatrains of that form.

furongloususong.summary: A seven-character quatrain. The poet sees a friend off at Hibiscus Tower. Cold rain and a lone hill give the parting its chill, and he asks the friend to carry a message: if relatives ask after him, say that his heart is like ice in a jade pot.
furongloususong.translation:
Cold rain joined the river and came to Wu in the night,
At dawn I see my guest off, the hills of Chu stand alone.
If friends and family in Luoyang should ask after me,
Tell them: a piece of ice in a jade pot is my heart.

glossary.note: A tower at Runzhou (present-day Zhenjiang, Jiangsu). Its site lay to the north-west of the city.
Daybreak.
Hills in the region of Chu. Runzhou belonged to Wu in ancient times, and it also bordered the Chu lands.

glossary.en: bing xin yu hu - 'an ice heart in a jade pot'
glossary.note: A comparison for a pure heart and a lofty character.

furongloususong.background: Written when Wang Changling had been demoted to be assistant magistrate of Jiangning. Xin Jian was a friend who was about to return north to Luoyang. In the last line, 「一片冰心在玉壺」, the poet speaks for his own clear conscience.

huanghelousong.summary: A seven-character quatrain. Li Bai sees Meng Haoran off at Yellow Crane Tower, as he sails down to Yangzhou in the misty blossom of the third month. In the last two lines he watches the single sail go, until only the Yangtze is left flowing to the edge of the sky. The feeling lingers.
huanghelousong.translation:
My old friend takes leave of Yellow Crane Tower to the west,
In the misty flowers of the third month he goes down to Yangzhou.
The far shadow of a lone sail vanishes in the blue hills,
I see only the Yangtze flowing to the rim of the sky.

glossary.note: Here it means Meng Haoran.
A phrase for spring, when blossoms are so thick that the landscape seems wrapped in mist.
An old name for Yangzhou.

glossary.en: tian ji - 'the edge of the sky'
glossary.note: The horizon.

huanghelousong.background: By Li Bai, around the year 728, when Meng Haoran left Wuchang for the east and Li Bai saw him off at Yellow Crane Tower. Meng Haoran was twelve years older than Li Bai, and Li Bai held him in great respect.

huixiangouShu.summary: A seven-character quatrain. The poet left home young and returns old: his accent has not changed, but the hair at his temples has thinned and whitened. Children who do not know him ask, laughing, where the guest has come from. The poem quietly shows how things change and time passes.
huixiangouShu.translation:
I left home young and have come back old,
My home accent unchanged, the hair at my temples thin.
The children meet me and do not know who I am,
They ask with a smile where the visitor has come from.

glossary.note: Jotted down on a passing impulse.
Youth.

glossary.en: bin mao shuai - 'the temple hair is thin'
glossary.note: The hair at the temples has grown sparse. The last character is read cui here.
A visitor from outside.

huixiangouShu.background: He Zhizhang was a poet of the early and High Tang. He left his native Yuezhou in youth and, in old age, resigned his office and went home, where he wrote this poem.

boqinhuai.summary: A seven-character quatrain. The poet moors at night by the Qinhuai River and hears singing girls performing a song of a fallen kingdom. They know nothing of the grief of a lost state, and the poem uses this to rebuke rulers who give themselves to pleasure and neglect the country.
boqinhuai.translation:
Mist wraps the cold water, moonlight wraps the sand,
At night I moor on the Qinhuai, close by a tavern.
The singing girls do not know the grief of a ruined state,
Across the river they are still singing 'Flowers in the Back Courtyard'.

glossary.note: A river through Nanjing, a place of wealth and pleasure from the Six Dynasties period onward.
Girls who sing for a living.

glossary.en: Hou ting hua - 'Flowers in the Back Courtyard'
glossary.note: The song 'Jade Trees, Flowers in the Back Courtyard', written by the last ruler of the Chen dynasty (557-589) of the Southern Dynasties, and thought of as the music of a doomed state.
To envelop, to cover over.

boqinhuai.background: By Du Mu. In his time, the late Tang, military governors held much of the country and the dynasty was weak. Du Mu uses the history of the Chen ruler, who lost his kingdom through dissipation, as a hint to his own age.

jiangnanfeng.summary: A seven-character quatrain. In the south of the Yangtze the poet meets Li Guinian, a musician who has fallen on hard times. He remembers how often he saw and heard him in the age of splendour, and now they meet again when the blossoms are falling. The contrast between then and now holds a sigh over the rise and fall of the world.
jiangnanfeng.translation:
In the house of the Prince of Qi I often saw you,
In front of Cui Jiu's hall I heard you more than once.
It is just the finest season of the southern land,
And in the time of falling flowers I meet you again.

glossary.note: A celebrated court musician under Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang. After the An Lushan rebellion he drifted to the south of the Yangtze.
Li Fan, a younger brother of Emperor Xuanzong, who loved music.
Cui Di, an official in the palace, who also loved music.

glossary.en: luo hua shi jie - 'the season of falling blossoms'
glossary.note: Late spring, and also a hint of a declining age.

jiangnanfeng.background: Du Fu wrote this in his last years, around 770, when he met Li Guinian at Tanzhou (now Changsha, Hunan). Some think it is among the last poems he wrote.

jiuyuejiuri.summary: A seven-character quatrain written on the Double Ninth Festival. Alone in a strange land, the poet longs for his brothers at home and imagines them climbing the hill with cornelian cherry sprigs in their hair, one person short. The phrase 'doubly' is where the traveller's homesickness is felt most truly.
jiuyuejiuri.translation:
Alone, a stranger in a strange land,
every festival day I miss my family twice as much.
Far away I know my brothers are climbing the heights,
each with a sprig of dogwood in his hair - and one person missing.

glossary.note: Here it means the land east of Mount Hua, not the modern province of Shandong. Wang Wei's home, Puzhou (today's Yongji in Shanxi), lay east of Mount Hua.

glossary.en: yi ke - 'a guest in a strange place'
glossary.note: Someone staying as a stranger far from home.
A fragrant plant. On the Double Ninth people wore sprigs of it to ward off evil. Pronounced zhu yu.
A custom of the Double Ninth Festival, the ninth day of the ninth month: families climb a hill or tower together.

jiuyuejiuri.background: Wang Wei wrote this at seventeen (some say fifteen) while in Chang'an, the Tang capital, far from his family. The Double Ninth Festival is the day for climbing a height and wearing cornelian cherry sprigs, so it is a day for families to be together.

weichengqu.summary: A seven-character quatrain seeing off a friend, Yuan the Second, who is posted to Anxi. Morning rain and fresh willows set a clean, bright scene of parting, and the last two lines press one more cup of wine on him, which says how hard it is to let him go.
weichengqu.translation:
In Weicheng the morning rain has settled the light dust,
by the inn the willows are green, their colour newly washed.
I urge you to drain one more cup of wine -
west of the Yang Pass there will be no old friends.

glossary.note: The old Qin-dynasty city of Xianyang, in today's Shaanxi. It was the usual place to see off travellers heading west.
To wet or moisten. Pronounced yi (falling tone).
A lodging house for travellers.
A frontier pass south-west of today's Dunhuang in Gansu. Beyond it lay the Western Regions, the lands of Central Asia.

weichengqu.background: Wang Wei's poem was originally titled 'Seeing Off Yuan the Second on a Mission to Anxi'. It was later set to music as 'Three Refrains on the Yang Pass' (Yangguan Sandie) and became the best-known parting song in Chinese.

wuyixiang.summary: A seven-character quatrain written on a visit to Wuyi Lane in Jinling (Nanjing). Wild grass by the bridge and a slanting sun at the lane's mouth show how far this once grand district has fallen, and swallows entering common homes hint at how the world has changed.
wuyixiang.translation:
By Zhuque Bridge, wild grass and flowers;
at the mouth of Wuyi Lane, the evening sun slants low.
The swallows that once nested before the halls of the Wangs and the Xies
now fly into the homes of ordinary people.

glossary.note: A lane south of the Qinhuai River in today's Nanjing. In the Eastern Jin dynasty (317-420) great families such as those of Wang Dao and Xie An lived here.
A bridge over the Qinhuai River, next to Wuyi Lane.

glossary.en: Wang Xie - 'the Wangs and the Xies'
glossary.note: The two most powerful aristocratic clans of the Eastern Jin dynasty: the family of Wang Dao and the family of Xie An.
Common, everyday.

wuyixiang.background: This is one of Liu Yuxi's 'Five Poems on Jinling'. By using the swallows as his image, he says that great families fall and times change without once saying so directly, and the feeling runs deep.

chibi.summary: A seven-character quatrain. At the old battlefield of Red Cliff the poet picks up a broken halberd, and it makes him think of the Three Kingdoms. If the east wind had not helped Zhou Yu, he supposes, the two Qiao sisters would be locked up in Cao Cao's Bronze Sparrow Terrace. Under the history lies a comment on the present: talent goes unrecognised, and even heroes need luck.
chibi.translation:
A broken halberd lies sunk in the sand, its iron not yet eaten away;
I polish and wash it myself and make out that it is from an earlier dynasty.
Had the east wind not favoured Zhou Yu,
in the deep spring the Bronze Sparrow Terrace would have locked in the two Qiaos.

glossary.note: A halberd (ji) was an ancient weapon, a long shaft with a blade and a side hook.
To be eaten away, to rust and rot.
Zhou Yu, a famous general of Wu in the Three Kingdoms period, who led the Wu forces at the Battle of Red Cliff.
The Bronze Sparrow Terrace, built by Cao Cao at Ye city. The 'two Qiaos' were the two daughters of Lord Qiao of Jiangdong: the elder married Sun Ce, the younger married Zhou Yu.

chibi.background: Du Mu wrote this while governor of Huangzhou, around 842. He liked to talk about military affairs, and here he reads a large history from a small find, judging events by imagining how they might have gone otherwise.

qiuxi.summary: A seven-character quatrain about the lonely life of a palace lady on an autumn night: silver candle, painted screen, a small fan swatting fireflies, and at last the night cool as water, as she lies alone looking up at the Herd Boy and Weaving Girl stars. Her sorrow is shown without being named.

glossary.note: A white candle, or a candle in a silver holder.

glossary.en: qing luo xiao shan - 'small fan of light silk'
glossary.note: A small fan made of thin, light silk gauze.
The steps of the palace. Some texts read 'palace street' instead.

glossary.en: Qianniu Zhinu - 'Herd Boy and Weaving Girl'
glossary.note: Two stars (Altair and Vega) from the old legend of lovers kept apart by the Milky Way, who may meet only once a year. They stand for lovers who cannot be together.

qiuxi.background: The poem is by Du Mu, though some attribute it to Wang Jian. It is a 'palace lament' poem, yet the word for grief never appears: the scenery alone suggests it.

yeyujibei.summary: A seven-character quatrain written to a loved one far away. Asked when he will return, he says there is no date yet; around him, night rain in the Ba hills fills the autumn pools. He then imagines a future reunion, trimming the candle by the west window, so past and future meet and the feeling is deep but gently put.
yeyujibei.translation:
You ask when I will come home - there is no date yet;
night rain on the Ba hills swells the autumn pools.
When can we trim the candle together by the west window
and talk back to this time, the night rain on the Ba hills?

glossary.note: Sent to someone in the north. Here the person is the poet's wife or family, far away to the north.
A general name for the hills of eastern Sichuan.
A pond in autumn.
To snip off the burnt wick so the flame burns brighter. It suggests sitting up late in long talk.

yeyujibei.background: Li Shangyin wrote this while living in Ba-Shu (Sichuan). It is also titled 'Sent to My Wife on a Night of Rain'. The phrase 'night rain on the Ba hills' appears twice, once for the present and once for the future, which is a neat piece of structure.

change.summary: A seven-character quatrain. Alone late into the night, the poet sees candle shadow, the Milky Way and the fading morning star, and thinks of Chang'e, who stole the elixir and flew to the moon, lonely for ever. Through her he speaks of his own loneliness.
change.translation:
The mica screen is deep in candle shadow;
the long river of stars slowly sinks, the morning star goes down.
Chang'e must regret that she stole the elixir -
sea of blue, sky of blue, night after night her heart alone.

glossary.note: A screen inlaid with mica, a shimmering, translucent mineral.
The Milky Way.

glossary.en: xiao xing chen - 'the morning star sinks'
glossary.note: The stars of early morning fade from sight as dawn comes.
In legend, the herb of immortality that the archer Hou Yi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West. Chang'e, his wife, stole it.

change.background: By Li Shangyin. Readers have long argued over what it means: a poem about Chang'e, a lament for a dead wife, or a poem of self-pity. The legend of Chang'e stealing the elixir and flying to the moon is told in the Huainanzi, a Han-dynasty book.

chuzhouxijian.summary: A seven-character quatrain. The poet loves the quiet grass beside a mountain stream and the orioles singing in deep trees. In the evening the spring flood comes fast with rain, and at a deserted ferry a small boat lies across the water by itself. The calm scene carries a plain, easy mood with a touch of solitude.
chuzhouxijian.translation:
I love, alone, the quiet grass growing by the stream,
and above it the yellow orioles singing in the deep trees.
The spring flood, bringing rain, runs faster as evening comes;
at the wild ferry no one is about, and the boat lies crosswise by itself.

glossary.note: Today's Chuzhou in Anhui province.
A mountain stream west of Chuzhou city. Some say it is the Shangma River.
The yellow oriole, a songbird.
A ferry crossing in the empty countryside.

chuzhouxijian.background: Wei Yingwu wrote this while governor of Chuzhou. His poetry is plain, quiet and far-reaching, and this poem is seen as his best.

chunwang.summary: A five-character regular poem. Trapped in Chang'an during the An Lushan rebellion, the poet sees the city desolate in spring, grieves for the state of the country and longs for his family. He ends with his thin grey hair, too sparse to hold a hairpin - a line of deep pain.

glossary.note: Refers to the fall of Chang'an to the rebel army.
Grieving over what is happening to the country.
The fires of war. Beacon fires were lit on towers to give warning of attack.
'Simply about to'. The word hun means 'almost' or 'quite'.
A long pin that men and women of old used to fix their hair knot, or a cap, in place.

chunwang.background: Du Fu wrote this in the spring of 757 (the second year of Zhide), when the rebels had trapped him in Chang'an. Regular five-character poems are known for their exact parallelism: the first four lines paint the scene and feeling, the last four express what is on the poet's heart.

shanjuqiuming.summary: A five-character regular poem about a mountain dwelling at an autumn dusk, just after fresh rain: bright moon among the pines, clear spring over the stones, bamboo rustling as the washerwomen return, lotus leaves stirring as the fishing boats go out. The last couplet says the poet is happy to stay, and shows the calm of a life in retirement.

glossary.note: Evening, when the light grows dim.
A woman washing clothes. The character huan is pronounced huan (falling tone).
To wither away and be gone.
A young man of noble family. Here the poet means himself.

shanjuqiuming.background: Late in life Wang Wei lived in retirement at Wangchuan, and this poem paints a fresh picture of life in the hills in autumn. The last line borrows from an old poem in the Chuci anthology, 'Summoning the Recluse', which calls a young nobleman to come home because spring grass is growing. Wang Wei turns the meaning round: spring has faded, but he will stay.

guoguren.summary: A five-character regular poem. The poet accepts an invitation to the farmhouse of an old friend. He describes the simple meal, the green trees round the village, the green hills outside the town wall, and talk of mulberry and hemp. At the end he promises to return on the Double Ninth to enjoy the chrysanthemums. It shows plain friendship and the pleasure of country life.
guoguren.translation:
My old friend has prepared chicken and millet
and invited me to his farmhouse.
Green trees close round the edge of the village;
blue hills slant beyond the town wall.
We open the window facing the threshing ground and vegetable garden,
and, wine cup in hand, talk of mulberry and hemp.
When the Double Ninth Festival comes,
I will come back to enjoy the chrysanthemums.

glossary.note: A chicken killed and cooked with millet rice. It stands for the simple meal a farm family offers a guest.
The outer wall of a town. Here it means the area beyond the village.

glossary.en: chang pu - 'threshing ground and vegetable garden'
glossary.note: The open yard where grain is threshed, and the kitchen garden.
The plants of silk and cloth, which stand for farm work in general.
The word jiu here means to draw near or to enjoy; it means drinking chrysanthemum wine and admiring the flowers.

guoguren.background: Meng Haoran wrote this while living in retirement at Xiangyang. The 'old friend' is the owner of the farm. The whole poem is plain and natural, and shows country life as it really is.

songdushaofu.summary: A five-character regular poem seeing off a friend who is going to take up an official post in Shuzhou. The poet does not speak of sadness; he encourages his friend instead: wherever one has a true friend, the ends of the earth are like next door, so do not weep at the fork in the road like young lovers. The mood is open and broad and washes away the usual bitterness of parting poems.
songdushaofu.translation:
The palace towers are guarded by the Three Qin;
through wind and mist I gaze towards the Five Fords.
The feeling in our parting
is the same: we are both men who travel for office.
Within the four seas, if one has a friend who knows him,
the ends of the earth are like a neighbour's door.
So do not stand at the fork in the road
and wet your sleeves with tears like boys and girls.

glossary.note: Another name for the county commandant, a local official in charge of law and order.
The Guanzhong region. After defeating the Qin dynasty (221-206 BC), Xiang Yu split the Qin lands into three kingdoms.
Five river crossings on the Min River. The name stands for the region of Shu (Sichuan).
To leave home and travel in order to take up an official post.
A close neighbour.

songdushaofu.background: Wang Bo was one of the 'Four Heroes of the Early Tang'. Du Shaofu was his friend, appointed county commandant of Shuzhou (today's Chongzhou in Sichuan). The couplet about a friend who knows you, with the ends of the earth like a neighbour's door, is a famous line that has lasted for ages.

dengyueyanglou.summary: A five-character regular poem. The first half shows the vast Lake Dongting seen from Yueyang Tower; the second half gives the poet's own sorrow - old, ill, drifting, without news of family, with war still raging on the northern passes. The wide view and the heavy heart set each other off.

glossary.note: To crack or burst open. Pronounced che (falling tone).
Qian and kun are the first two hexagrams of the Book of Changes, standing for heaven and earth.
Horses of war, used as a word for war itself.
Leaning on the railing or window-sill of the tower.
Tears and runny nose; it means weeping bitterly.

dengyueyanglou.background: Du Fu wrote this in the winter of 768 (the third year of Dali) when he climbed Yueyang Tower in Yuezhou. He was old and ill and drifting in the region of the Xiang River. The couplet about Wu and Chu splitting and heaven and earth floating is a famous description of Lake Dongting.

lvyeshuhuai.summary: A five-character regular poem. The poet's boat is moored by the river bank at night. He sees fine grass in a light breeze, then stars hanging over a wide plain and the moon surging on the great river; this grand scene is set against his own old age, illness and loneliness, like a single sand gull. It speaks of a life adrift and desolate.
lvyeshuhuai.translation:
Fine grass, a light breeze on the bank;
a tall mast, a lone boat in the night.
Stars hang down, the open plain is wide;
the moon pours forth, the great river flows.
Is my name made by my writings?
My office must end because I am old and ill.
Drifting, drifting - what am I like?
Between heaven and earth, one sand gull.

glossary.note: The tall mast of a boat.
The stars seem to hang low at the edge of the sky over the wide land.
The moonlight seems to surge along with the river water.
To make a name. Pronounced zhu (falling tone).
A gull that rests on sandbanks.

lvyeshuhuai.background: In 765 (the first year of Yongtai) Du Fu left Chengdu and went down the Yangtze, and wrote this on the way. The pair of lines about stars hanging over the plain and the moon surging in the river has been admired for ages.

songyouren.summary: A five-character regular poem about seeing off a friend, with green hills and white water around the town and the friend leaving like a lone tumbleweed. The middle lines compare the traveller's mind to a drifting cloud and the friend's feeling to the setting sun. It ends with a wave of the hand and the whinny of a horse, and the feeling lingers.

glossary.note: The outer wall of the town on its north side.
A lone tumbleweed, blown about by the wind. It stands for a wanderer without a settled home.

glossary.en: ban ma - 'a horse parting from its herd'
glossary.note: A horse separated from its companions.
The sound of a horse neighing.
From this point on.

songyouren.background: Li Bai wrote this, but we do not know who the friend was or where they parted. The pairs of lines are balanced in a natural way and the feeling is held back; it is one of Li Bai's best five-character regular poems.

yueyejishe.summary: A five-character regular poem. On an autumn night in wartime the poet hears the garrison drum and the cry of a lone wild goose, and thinks of his brothers, scattered by the war. He laments that letters do not arrive and the fighting does not stop. In 'the moon is brighter at home' he puts his homesickness.

glossary.note: A modest way of saying 'my own younger brother'.
The drum sounded by soldiers on frontier guard duty to mark the night watches.

glossary.en: lu cong jin ye bai - 'the dew turns white from tonight'
glossary.note: It was the time of the White Dew solar term, in early autumn, when dew forms heavily.
Letters often fail to arrive.

glossary.en: wei xiu bing - 'the war has not ended'
glossary.note: The fighting is not yet over.

yueyejishe.background: Du Fu wrote this in the autumn of 759 (the second year of Qianyuan) at Qinzhou (today's Tianshui in Gansu). The An Lushan rebellion had scattered him and his brothers.

linDongting.summary: A five-character regular poem sent to a high minister. The first four lines show Lake Dongting in the eighth month, vast and powerful. The last four use the images of having no boat to cross and envying the fish to say that the poet hopes to take office, asking the minister for an introduction without grovelling.

glossary.note: The lake holds the sky, because the surface mirrors it.
The sky.
A great marsh of ancient times, in today's Hubei and Hunan.
To cross a river or lake.
From the Huainanzi: 'Standing at the river and envying the fish is not as good as going home and weaving a net.' It stands for wanting to do something.

linDongting.background: Meng Haoran wrote this; the 'Prime Minister Zhang' is Zhang Jiuling. It is a poem of the kind written to ask a patron for an introduction to an official post.

dujingmen.summary: A five-character regular poem. Leaving Shu and going east, the poet passes Jingmen and sees the wide plain and the river rushing on, the moon like a mirror from heaven and clouds that build a mirage. He ends by cherishing the water of his home, which sees his boat off for ten thousand li, and so shows his love of his native place.
dujingmen.translation:
I have come a long way, crossing beyond Jingmen,
to roam in the land of Chu.
The mountains end as the plain spreads flat;
the river runs on into the great wilderness.
Under the moon it is a mirror flown from heaven;
clouds rise and build towers above the sea.
Still I love the water of my old home,
which sees my boat off for ten thousand li.

glossary.note: Mount Jingmen in today's Yidu in Hubei, the first mountain the Yangtze meets after it leaves the Three Gorges.
A wide, open stretch of country.
The moon, seen as a mirror that has flown down from the sky.
A mirage, a city or towers seen above the sea or in the air.

glossary.en: gu xiang shui - 'the water of my old home'
glossary.note: The Yangtze, which flows down from Shu (Sichuan), the poet's home region.

dujingmen.background: Li Bai wrote this around the age of twenty-four (724, the twelfth year of Kaiyuan) when he left Shu and travelled east. The poem is full of a young man's high spirits and his attachment to home.

cibeigushan.summary: A five-character regular poem written on a boat journey. The poet describes the wide river and the fresh sense of sunrise and spring on the water, and in the last couplet, seeing wild geese go home, he wishes to send a letter to his family far away. The lines about the sun rising out of the last of the night and spring entering the old year are famous.

glossary.note: A hill in today's Zhenjiang in Jiangsu, standing on the Yangtze.
The sun rising over the sea.

glossary.en: can ye - 'the last of the night'
glossary.note: The night that is nearly over.

glossary.en: ru jiu nian - 'enters the old year'
glossary.note: The breath of spring arrives before the old year has ended.
A letter to or from one's family.

cibeigushan.background: Wang Wan was a poet of the High Tang. The poem is included in the anthology 'Heroic Spirits of the Rivers and Mountains' (Hean Yingling Ji) under the title 'Thoughts of Jiangnan', and is his best-known work.

huanghelou.summary: A seven-character regular poem. The first half uses the legend of Yellow Crane Tower: the immortal has gone, the tower is empty, the clouds are far away. The second half turns to the clear river, the grass and the distant shore, and ends in homesickness at dusk, with mist on the water that brings sorrow. The poem flows with great force and is held to be one of the finest Tang poems in this form.

glossary.note: A tower on Snake Hill in today's Wuhan. By legend an immortal once passed here riding a yellow crane.
Clear and sharp to see.
A town on the north bank of the Yangtze, now a district of Wuhan.
Grass growing richly.
A sandbar in the Yangtze near Wuchang. It is named after the 'Rhapsody on a Parrot' by Mi Heng, who is said to have been buried there.

huanghelou.background: Cui Hao wrote this. The story is told that Li Bai climbed Yellow Crane Tower, saw Cui Hao's poem and put down his brush, saying there was a scene before his eyes he could not put into words, because Cui Hao had already written a poem above.

denggao.summary: A seven-character regular poem. On the Double Ninth the poet climbs a height and sees the bleak, vast river in autumn. He mourns years of wandering as a guest far from home, and ends with 'hardship, bitter regret, frosty hair' - deep and sorrowful. Many call it the finest poem of its form.

glossary.note: A small sandbar or island in the water.
Trees that are shedding their leaves.
A whole life.

glossary.en: fan shuang bin - 'thick frost on the temples'
glossary.note: Hair at the temples that has turned white as frost.
Just recently given up (drinking).

denggao.background: Du Fu wrote this in 767 (the second year of Dali) on the Double Ninth, climbing a height at Kuizhou (today's Fengjie in Chongqing). Every line of this poem keeps to parallelism, which is why it is held to be the perfect example of a regular seven-character poem.

dengfenghuangtai.summary: A regulated poem with seven characters to the line. Standing on Phoenix Terrace in Jinling (Nanjing), Li Bai moves from the empty terrace and the faded glory of the Wu and Jin courts to reflections on the rise and fall of dynasties. The last couplet turns personal: clouds hide the sun, he cannot see Chang'an, and he is sad.

glossary.note: A terrace in present-day Nanjing. Tradition says it was built in the Southern Dynasties period (the Liu Song, 5th century) after phoenix-like birds were seen gathering there.
A way of referring to scholar-officials and nobles, who were recognised by their official dress.
A mountain with three peaks on the bank of the Yangtze, south-west of Nanjing.
The Qinhuai River splits into two branches as it reaches Nanjing.
A sandbank in the Yangtze at Nanjing.

dengfenghuangtai.background: Li Bai wrote this while wandering around Jinling after he had been sent away from the Tang court with a present of gold. Nanjing was the capital of Wu, of Eastern Jin and of other southern dynasties. It is generally thought that the poem imitates Cui Hao's 'Yellow Crane Tower', a famous poem of the same period. In the last couplet the sun stands for the emperor and the clouds for the courtiers who hide him, so the line carries Li Bai's grief at being far from the capital.

jinse.summary: A regulated poem in which the fifty strings of an ornate zither call up memories of the past. The middle four lines pile up four allusions - Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, the cuckoo, the pearl-tears, the jade-mist - that are hazy and hard to pin down. The ending sighs that the past was already a daze even while it was happening. Readers have taken the poem as mourning a wife, as lamenting the poet's own life, or as a poem about an object.

glossary.note: It means without any cause. The poet wonders why the zither has so many strings, as if the instrument itself were stirring up his feelings.
The best years of life, that is, one's youth.

glossary.en: Zhuang sheng xiao meng mi hu die - 'Zhuangzi, in a morning dream, lost in a butterfly'
glossary.note: From the Zhuangzi, in the chapter on the equality of things. Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell whether he was a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming of being a man.
Du Yu, ruler of the ancient state of Shu. Legend says that after he died his spirit became a cuckoo, whose cry in spring sounds like longing and regret.
A feeling of being at a loss, as if something has been taken away.

jinse.background: By Li Shangyin, one of his best-known poems. Because the images are so hazy, readers have long disagreed about what it means. It is also very influential, and shows the delicate, beauty-loving style of late Tang poetry (the 9th century).

wuti1.summary: A regulated poem about love. Meeting is hard and parting harder. The silkworm and the candle are images of devotion that lasts until death, and the poem ends on a thread of hope as the poet asks the Blue Bird to carry word.

glossary.note: Poems for which the poet chose not to give a title. They are mostly about love or about his own life and fortunes.
The word for silk sounds like the word for longing, so 'the silkworm spins silk until it dies' also means that longing lasts until death. This is a pun that works only in Chinese.
Here the wax that runs down the candle. It also stands for tears of the eyes.
A legendary island mountain of the immortals, far away over the sea. It stands here for the place where the beloved lives.
In legend, the messenger of the Queen Mother of the West. It became the usual image for a bearer of news between lovers.

wuti1.background: Li Shangyin's 'Untitled' poems mostly deal with love and with his own feelings about his life, in a tender and veiled style. In this poem the couplet about the silkworm and the candle has become a famous saying for steadfast devotion and for giving oneself until the end.

wuti2.summary: A regulated poem. The first four lines recall seeing a beloved at a banquet last night: the two cannot fly together like phoenixes, but their hearts understand each other. The next two lines describe the lively party games. The ending sighs that at dawn he must go to his post, drifting like a tumbleweed.
wuti2.translation:
Last night the stars, last night the wind,
West of the painted tower, east of the Hall of Cassia.
I have no wings like the coloured phoenix, to fly side by side with you,
But my heart has a spirit-horn of the rhinoceros, one point that runs through.
Across the seats we passed the hook, and the spring wine was warm;
In teams we guessed the covered object, and the wax lamps were red.
Alas, I hear the drum and must go to my post;
Riding to Orchid Terrace, I am like a tumbleweed blown about.

glossary.note: People said the white lines in a rhinoceros horn ran right through from one end to the other, so the horn became an image for two hearts that understand each other without words.
A party game in which a hook is passed from hand to hand under the table, and a guesser tries to say who is holding it.
A guessing game in which something is covered up and the players try to name it, often with verse clues.
The imperial library of the Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD). In the Tang its role was held by the Palace Library (Mishusheng), where Li Shangyin served as a proofreader.
A dry plant that blows about in the wind. It is the usual image for a person who has no settled place.

wuti2.background: By Li Shangyin, probably written while he was working in the Palace Library. The couplet about wings and the rhinoceros horn is one of his most widely quoted lines.

shuxiang.summary: A regulated poem. Du Fu visits the shrine of Zhuge Liang in Chengdu and moves from the shrine's quiet scenery to Zhuge Liang's service to two rulers. The last couplet, on the chancellor dying before his campaign could succeed, expresses deep sorrow for a hero whose work was left unfinished.

glossary.note: Zhuge Liang, chancellor of the kingdom of Shu-Han in the Three Kingdoms period (3rd century). He is remembered as the model of a loyal and gifted minister.
Another name for Chengdu, the capital of Shu. It is named for the office that once managed its famous brocade.

glossary.en: san gu pin fan - 'three visits, again and again'
glossary.note: Liu Bei visited Zhuge Liang in his hut three times to ask for his help, and later consulted him repeatedly. Pinfan means 'time after time'.

glossary.en: liang chao kai ji - 'opening the way for two reigns'
glossary.note: He helped Liu Bei to found the state, and then helped Liu Bei's son Liu Shan to carry it on.

glossary.en: chu shi wei jie - 'the campaign did not succeed'
glossary.note: Zhuge Liang led several northern campaigns against the rival state of Wei. He died in the field in 234 before he could win.

shuxiang.background: Du Fu came to Chengdu in the early spring of 760 and wrote this after visiting the Wuhou Shrine, the temple to Zhuge Liang. Du Fu had the deepest respect for Zhuge Liang, a man who gave his whole life to his ruler's cause.

kezhi.summary: A regulated poem about the joy of a visit and the simple welcome the host can give. Spring water surrounds the house and gulls come every day. The flowery path is swept and the thatch gate opened for the guest. The food is plain and the wine is old, but he still invites his neighbour to drink with them. The poem shows warm, honest hospitality.

glossary.note: A path covered with fallen petals.
A gate made of woven twigs and grass. It describes the home of a poor family.
The food on the plate. The second character is read sun.
Unfiltered wine brewed in an earlier year.
The wine that is left over.

kezhi.background: Du Fu wrote this at his thatched cottage in Chengdu. A note on the poem's original title says it was written in joy at a visit from Magistrate Cui, the county magistrate who was the guest. The poem is full of friendly details of everyday life.

wenguanjun.summary: A regulated poem. Du Fu hears that the government army has retaken Henan and Hebei, which means the An Lushan Rebellion is nearly over. He goes from tears of surprise to wild joy, packing up his books and planning the journey home. The poem is lively and free, a rare cheerful piece among Du Fu's works.
wenguanjun.translation:
Beyond Sword Pass, news suddenly comes that Jibei has been retaken;
When I first hear it, my tears soak my clothes.
I turn to look at my wife and children - where has their sorrow gone?
I roll up my books of poems at random, almost mad with joy.
By day I must sing aloud and drink my fill;
With green spring for company, it is a good time to go home.
I will go at once from Ba Gorge through Wu Gorge,
Then down to Xiangyang and on towards Luoyang.

glossary.note: The land south of Sword Pass (Jianmen), that is, the region of Shu in present-day Sichuan, where Du Fu was living.
The northern part of present-day Hebei, the base from which the rebels of the An Lushan Rebellion had operated.
To roll up without care or order, which suggests how happy and hurried he is.

glossary.en: Ba xia, Wu xia - 'Ba Gorge, Wu Gorge'
glossary.note: Two of the Three Gorges of the Yangtze, the river route out of Sichuan.
A city in present-day Hubei, on the way from the Yangtze towards the north.

wenguanjun.background: In the spring of 763 Du Fu was in Zizhou (present-day Santai in Sichuan) when he heard that Shi Chaoyi, the last rebel leader, had been defeated and had killed himself, so the An Lushan Rebellion was largely over. He wrote this poem at once. Later critics called it a 'fast poem', a rare happy and quick-flowing one among Du Fu's poems.

xisaishan.summary: A regulated poem. Liu Yuxi visits Xisai Mountain and looks back at the Jin conquest of Wu: not even iron chains across the river could stop the invading fleet. He sighs over the rise and fall of states, and ends by noting that the empire is now united and only rustling reeds remain where the old fort stood. The poem speaks of the present through the past, as a lesson from history.
xisaishan.translation:
Wang Jun's tower ships came down from Yizhou,
And the royal aura of Jinling faded and went dark.
A thousand fathoms of iron chain sank to the river bed,
One surrender flag came out of Stone City.
How many times in the human world have men grieved over the past!
The mountain keeps its old shape, pillowed on the cold current.
Now that all within the four seas is one home,
The old ramparts in autumn hold only rustling reeds and rushes.

glossary.note: A mountain on the bank of the Yangtze at present-day Huangshi in Hubei. Its position made it a strategic fortress for centuries.
A general of the Western Jin dynasty (265-316). He led his fleet down the Yangtze from Yizhou (Sichuan) in 280 and destroyed the southern state of Wu.
The fortune or energy believed to attend a ruling house when it rises.
The flag raised in giving up. Here it is the flag of the last Wu ruler.
The camps and forts of earlier times, now ruined.

xisaishan.background: Liu Yuxi, a Tang poet, wrote this in 824 while passing Xisai Mountain on his way to take up the post of prefect of Hezhou. By recalling how the Jin destroyed Wu, the poem hints that the warlords who then held power in the provinces (the jiedushi, or military governors) could not last either.

wangyue.summary: An ancient-style poem (gushi) with five characters to the line. Du Fu looks at Mount Tai, first from far off, where the green of Qi and Lu seems endless, then close up, with the sharp line between light and shade and clouds that open the chest. He ends with the vow to climb to the very top. The poem is grand in manner and full of a young man's ambition.
wangyue.translation:
Mount Dai - how shall I describe it?
Green across Qi and Lu, without end.
Creation has gathered here all that is divine and lovely;
Yin and yang cut dusk from dawn.
Layered clouds rise and wash my chest clean;
I strain my eyes wide to follow the birds returning home.
One day I shall surely climb to the very top,
And see all the other mountains small below me.

glossary.note: Another name for Mount Tai in Shandong, the first of the Five Sacred Mountains and a place of imperial sacrifices.
Two ancient states. Qi lay to the north of Mount Tai and Lu to the south, so the phrase means the whole region.
Nature, the forces that make the world.
Literally, to split the corners of the eyes. It describes opening the eyes as wide as possible. The second character is read zi.
It means 'sooner or later I will certainly'. It states a firm intention.

wangyue.background: Du Fu wrote this early in life, while travelling through the lands of Qi and Zhao around 736, when he was in his twenties. It is one of his earliest surviving poems. The last line shows the young poet's ambition.

yuexiadouzhuo.summary: An ancient-style poem with five characters to the line. Li Bai drinks alone among the flowers, invites the moon and his own shadow to drink with him, and sings and dances with them. In the end he is still alone, and hopes to share an unattached friendship with them for ever and meet them in the Milky Way. The imagination is strange and free, and it shows loneliness and openness of heart side by side.

glossary.note: It means drinking by oneself, with a cup poured for oneself.
No close friend or companion is with him.

glossary.en: pai huai - 'to linger, to pace to and fro'
glossary.note: To move back and forth. The moon seems to hover as he sings.

glossary.en: wu qing you - 'a friendship beyond feeling'
glossary.note: Companionship that is not weighed down by the sentiments of the everyday world. The moon and shadow ask nothing of him.
The river of stars across the night sky, which is where the poet imagines meeting the moon again.

yuexiadouzhuo.background: This is the first of four poems on drinking alone under the moon by Li Bai. It was probably written around 744, in his Chang'an period, near the time when he was given gold and sent away from the court.

jiangjinjiu.summary: A yuefu song (a poem in the old folk-song form) with seven-character lines. Li Bai urges his friends to drink. The Yellow River and white hair stand for the shortness of life, so he says to enjoy the moment. He also boasts that Heaven made him for a purpose, and the last line, 'with you I will dissolve the sorrows of ten thousand ages', hides in its wildness the grief of a talent that was never used.
jiangjinjiu.translation:
Do you not see - the waters of the Yellow River come down from Heaven,
Rushing to the sea, never to return?
Do you not see - in the high hall, before the bright mirror, men grieve over white hair,
Black silk in the morning, snow by evening?
When life goes well, one must take one's fill of joy;
Do not let a golden cup stand empty facing the moon.
Heaven made me with talent, and it must be of use;
A thousand pieces of gold, once spent, will come back again.
Boil the mutton, slaughter the ox, and let us be merry;
We should drink three hundred cups in one go.
Master Cen, young Danqiu,
Bring on the wine; do not let your cups stop.
I will sing you a song;
Please turn your ears and listen to me.
Bells and drums and dishes of jade are not worth prizing;
I only wish to be drunk for ever and never wake.
Since ancient times the sages and worthies have all been lonely;
Only the drinkers have left their names behind.
The Prince of Chen once feasted at Pingle,
Wine at ten thousand a measure, joking and laughing as he pleased.
Why should the host say he has little money?
Just go and buy wine, and we will drink it face to face.
The five-flower horse, the fur worth a thousand gold -
Call the boy to take them out and trade them for fine wine,
And with you I will dissolve the sorrows of ten thousand ages.

glossary.note: An old title from the Han yuefu (folk-song bureau) collection, meaning 'please drink'. The first character is read qiang here, meaning 'please'.

glossary.en: Cen fu zi, Dan qiu sheng - 'Master Cen, young Danqiu'
glossary.note: Cen Xun and Yuan Danqiu, friends of Li Bai who drank with him.
Cao Zhi, the poet son of Cao Cao, who was enfeoffed as Prince of Chen. In one of his poems he wrote of coming home to feast at Pingle with wine at ten thousand a measure.
A prized horse whose coat has five patterns or dapples.

glossary.en: qian jin qiu - 'fur worth a thousand gold'
glossary.note: A fur robe of great value.

jiangjinjiu.background: Li Bai wrote this around 752, while drinking with Cen Xun and Yuan Danqiu at Yingyang. He had left Chang'an years before. His manner is bold and free, but behind it lies bitterness at not being employed for his talents.

xinglunan1.summary: A yuefu song with seven-character lines. Faced with a splendid feast, the poet cannot eat, because the road ahead is hard and he is lost. But recalling the examples of Jiang Taigong and Yi Yin, he steadies himself with the faith that 'a time will come when a long wind breaks the waves', showing that he still holds to his ideals.

glossary.note: A variant of the word 「饈」, meaning fine food.
Here it is used for the word 「值」, meaning to be worth a certain value.

glossary.en: chui diao bi xi - 'fishing on a green brook'
glossary.note: A reference to Jiang Taigong (Lu Shang), who as an old man fished on the Wei River until King Wen of Zhou found him and made him his adviser.

glossary.en: cheng zhou meng ri bian - 'riding a boat, dreaming of the side of the sun'
glossary.note: Legend says that Yi Yin, before he met Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BC), dreamed that he sailed in a boat past the sun. He later became Tang's great minister.

glossary.en: chang feng po lang - 'a long wind to break the waves'
glossary.note: From the Song Shu (History of the Song), the life of Zong Que, who said he wished to ride a long wind and break waves ten thousand li wide. It means a great ambition.

xinglunan1.background: The first of three poems titled 'The Road Is Hard' that Li Bai wrote when he left Chang'an, after he had been given gold and sent away. It shows his frustration at having his career blocked, yet his refusal to give up.

shudaonan.summary: A yuefu song with lines of uneven length. Li Bai pictures the wild danger of the road to Shu: ladders to the sky, plank roads on cliffs, gibbons afraid to climb, tigers and snakes. The refrain 'the road to Shu is hard, harder than climbing to the blue sky' keeps returning. The poem is grand in force, strange in imagination and free in language.
shudaonan.translation:
Ah! How perilous, how high!
The road to Shu is hard, harder than climbing to the blue sky!
Cancong and Yufu - how dim and distant the founding of their kingdom!
Since then forty-eight thousand years have passed,
And no human smoke has joined them to the passes of Qin.
To the west, facing Mount Taibai, there is a path only birds can take,
That can cut across the summit of Mount Emei.
The earth cracked and the mountains broke, and brave men died;
Only afterwards were sky-ladders and stone plank roads hooked together.
Above are the high peaks where the six dragons turn the sun back;
Below are whirling rivers where the surging waves run against themselves.
Even the yellow crane in flight cannot get across;
The gibbons and monkeys, wanting to go over, grieve at the climb.
How Qingni Ridge winds and winds!
In a hundred steps it bends nine times around the cliffs.
I touch the stars Shen and Jing, look up, and hold my breath;
I press my hand to my chest and sit sighing long.
I ask you, on this journey west, when will you come back?
The road is fearful, the rocks steep, and there is no climbing them.
You will only see sad birds crying in ancient trees,
The male flying, the female following, circling through the forest.
And you will hear the cuckoo crying under the night moon,
Grieving over the empty mountains.
The road to Shu is hard, harder than climbing to the blue sky;
To hear it would fade the colour from a young face!
Linked peaks are not a foot from the sky;
Withered pines hang upside down, leaning on sheer cliffs.
Flying rapids and waterfalls race each other in uproar,
Pounding the cliffs and turning boulders, thundering through ten thousand gorges.
Such is its danger -
Ah, you who have come from so far away, why have you come?
Sword Pavilion is steep and towering;
One man holds the pass, and ten thousand cannot break through.
If those who guard it are not trusted kin,
They may turn into wolves and jackals.
In the morning one avoids fierce tigers, in the evening long snakes;
They grind their teeth and drink blood, killing men like hemp.
Though Brocade City is said to be a place of pleasure,
It is better to go home early.
The road to Shu is hard, harder than climbing to the blue sky;
I turn my body to look west, and sigh long.

glossary.en: yi xu xi - an exclamation of wonder
glossary.note: An exclamation of wonder in the dialect of Shu (present-day Sichuan).

glossary.en: Can cong, Yu fu - 'Cancong and Yufu'
glossary.note: Legendary early rulers of the ancient state of Shu, so old that almost nothing was recorded about them.

glossary.en: liu long hui ri - 'six dragons turn the sun back'
glossary.note: In myth the sun god rides in a chariot drawn by six dragons. The peaks here are so high that even the chariot has to turn back.
A mountain pass in present-day Hui county in Gansu, a main route into Shu.
The cuckoo. Legend says it is the spirit of Du Yu, the old king of Shu, and its cry sounds like grief.
A narrow, steep pass in the north of present-day Jiange county in Sichuan, the key gateway to Shu.
Chengdu, the chief city of Shu.

shudaonan.background: Li Bai wrote this in the early Tianbao years (the 740s), around the time he went to Chang'an. One view is that it is a farewell to a friend travelling to Shu; another is that it has a hidden warning about the times. It is long and grand, and is regarded as the finest of Li Bai's yuefu poems.

tianmuyin.summary: A ge xing (song-style poem) with seven-character lines at its core. Li Bai describes a dream journey to Mount Tianmu in lavish, wonderful images: he flies over Mirror Lake by moonlight, climbs the mountain and sees the sun rise from the sea, meets thunder and lightning, and watches a cave-heaven open with its immortals. Then he wakes with a start. The ending, 'how could I bow and bend the waist to serve the powerful', is a statement of scorn for the high and mighty.

glossary.note: A mountain in present-day Zhejiang, east of Xinchang. The second character is read mu.
One of the legendary islands of the immortals in the eastern sea.
A lake at present-day Shaoxing in Zhejiang, also called Jian Lake.
Xie Lingyun, a poet of the Southern Dynasties (5th century) who loved mountain travel. He is said to have invented wooden clogs with removable teeth for climbing hills, and he visited Mount Tianmu.
A mythical rooster in the heavens. When it crows, all the roosters of the world crow after it.
A word for flashes of lightning.

glossary.en: cui mei zhe yao - 'bow the brows, bend the waist'
glossary.note: To lower the head and bend the back, that is, to behave humbly and servilely before people of power.

tianmuyin.background: Li Bai wrote this after he left Chang'an in the Tianbao years, as he prepared to travel to eastern Lu and to the regions of Wu and Yue. It is a farewell to friends, and is also known under the title 'Farewell to the Gentlemen of Eastern Lu'. The last line is a kind of confession of how he felt about powerful men.

chunjianghuayueye.summary: A ge xing in which the spring river, flowers and bright moon run through the whole poem. It begins with the moonlit river and sky, moves on to the shortness of human life against the endless river and moon, then to the longing of a wife and a traveller far apart, and ends with the slanting moon and the trees by the river. It has been called the one poem that stands above all the rest of Tang poetry.

glossary.note: It describes the look of light flashing on moving water.
Small bits of ice, like tiny hail. The moon on the flowers makes the whole wood look as if it were sprinkled with them. The word is read xian.
Flat ground by the water's edge, or a sandbar.
A place on the water around the Yangtze and Xiang rivers, shaded by maple trees. It is a stock setting for parting and sorrow.

glossary.en: bian zhou zi - 'the one in the small boat'
glossary.note: A traveller who goes away in a little boat.
The stone on which women beat laundry with a mallet. The sound of washing was a classic image of a woman missing a distant husband.

glossary.en: Jie shi, Xiao Xiang - 'Jieshi and Xiaoxiang'
glossary.note: Jieshi Mountain in the north and the Xiao and Xiang rivers in the south. Together they stand for the distance between north and south.

chunjianghuayueye.background: Zhang Ruoxu lived in the early Tang. Only two of his poems survive, and this is by far the better known. The modern scholar Wen Yiduo praised it as the 'poem of poems, the peak of peaks'. In the Qing dynasty (1644-1912) the writer Wang Kaiyun said it stands alone across the whole age, and later readers have kept using that praise.

changhenge.summary: Bai Juyi's long narrative poem, 'Song of Everlasting Sorrow', tells the love tragedy of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang and his consort Yang Guifei: her rise in favour, the An Lushan Rebellion, her forced death at Mawei Slope, the emperor's grief, the Daoist master's search for her, and her meeting with him in a mountain of immortals, where she sends tokens. It ends on 'this sorrow goes on and on, with no end in time', and mixes criticism with sympathy.
changhenge.translation:
The Han emperor prized beauty and longed for a woman who could topple a state;
for many years on the throne he sought her and could not find her.
In the Yang family was a girl just grown,
raised deep in the inner rooms, known to no one.
Born with a beauty she could not hide away,
one morning she was chosen to stand beside the ruler.
One backward glance and a smile, and a hundred charms were born;
the powdered and pencilled ladies of the six palaces lost their colour.
In the spring chill he bade her bathe in the Huaqing pool;
the warm spring water was smooth as it washed her skin, like congealed fat.
Maids helped her up, delicate and without strength -
this was the first time she received his favour.
Cloud-like hair, flower face, gold ornaments swaying;
in the warm hibiscus curtains they passed the spring nights.
The spring night is bitterly short, the sun was high when he rose;
from then on the ruler did not hold early court.
She took his joy and served at his feasts, never at leisure;
in spring she went with him on spring outings, at night she had the night to herself.
Among the beauties of the rear palaces were three thousand women,
and the favour of three thousand rested on one body.
In the golden house, her toilette done, she charmed him through the night;
when the feast in the jade tower ended, she was drunk with the spring.
Her sisters and brothers were all granted lands;
how enviable, the glory that rose at their gates.
It made the hearts of parents throughout the world
value the birth of daughters above the birth of sons.
The Li Palace rises high into the blue clouds;
immortal music drifts on the wind and is heard everywhere.
Slow song and slow dance, the strings and pipes held tight;
all day long the ruler watched and could not have enough.
Then the war drums of Yuyang came shaking the earth,
and broke into the tune of "Rainbow Skirts and Feathered Robes".
In the nine-fold city and its towers, smoke and dust rose;
a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen went to the south-west.
The kingfisher banners swayed, going on, then halting,
a hundred li and more west of the capital gate.
The six armies would not set out, and nothing could be done;
with her curved moth brows, she died in front of the horses.
Her flower ornaments lay on the ground, and no one gathered them,
kingfisher feathers, gold sparrows, jade hairpins.
The ruler covered his face and could not save her;
turning to look, blood and tears flowed together.
Yellow dust spread wide, the wind was bleak and cold;
on the winding plank road they climbed to Sword Gate Pass.
Below Mount Emei few people travelled;
the banners had no gleam, the sunlight was thin.
The river of Shu was green, the mountains of Shu blue;
the sage ruler's feeling was there each morning and each evening.
Seeing the moon from the travelling palace, a colour that wounds the heart;
hearing bells in the night rain, a sound that breaks the bowels.
Heaven turned, the sun came round, the dragon carriage returned;
at this place he hesitated and could not leave.
Below the slope of Mawei, in the mud and earth,
he saw no jade face, only the place where she died.
Ruler and ministers looked at each other, their clothes all wet;
gazing east to the capital gate, they let the horses find their way home.
Returned, the ponds and gardens were all as before,
the hibiscus of Taiye Pool and the willows of Weiyang.
The hibiscus is like her face, the willows like her brows;
facing this, how could he not let tears fall?
On a night when spring wind opens the peach and plum blossom,
in the season when autumn rain makes the wutong leaves fall.
In the Western Palace and the Southern Garden, much autumn grass;
fallen leaves fill the steps, red, and unswept.
The disciples of the Pear Garden, their hair newly white;
the attendants of the pepper chambers, their dark brows grown old.
In the evening hall fireflies fly, and he thinks in silence;
the lone lamp's wick trimmed to the end, and still he cannot sleep.
Slow, slow the bells and drums, the long night is just beginning;
bright, bright the River of Stars, the sky about to dawn.
The mandarin-duck tiles are cold, the frost heavy;
the kingfisher quilt is chill - who shares it with him?
Long, long they have been parted by life and death, year after year,
and her spirit has never once come into his dreams.
A Daoist from Linqiong, a guest at Hongdu,
could by utmost sincerity call back spirits.
Moved by the ruler's tossing, turning longing,
he had the master of arts search for her diligently.
Riding the void and driving the air, he sped like lightning,
rose to heaven and entered the earth, seeking her everywhere.
Above he went to the end of the blue void, below to the Yellow Springs;
in both places vast and dim, and he saw nothing.
Suddenly he heard that there is an immortal mountain on the sea,
and that the mountain lies between the empty and the faint.
Towers and pavilions, delicate and fine, five-coloured clouds rising;
within are many graceful immortals.
Among them is one whose courtesy name is Taizhen,
snow-white skin, flower face - it seemed to be she.
At the west wing of the golden gate he knocked on the jade door,
and had Xiaoyu pass word to Shuangcheng.
Hearing that an envoy had come from the Son of Heaven of Han,
inside the nine-flowered curtains her dreaming soul started.
She gathered her robe, pushed aside the pillow, rose and paced about;
the pearl blinds and silver screens opened one after another.
Her cloud-like hair half askew, newly woken from sleep,
her flower crown unsettled, she came down the hall.
The wind blew her immortal sleeves, floating upward,
still like the dance of "Rainbow Skirts and Feathered Robes".
Her jade face was quiet and sad, her tears streaming;
a spray of pear blossom, in spring, carrying rain.
Full of feeling, with a fixed gaze, she thanked the ruler:
since parting, voice and face have both been dim and far.
In the Zhaoyang Hall, favour and love were cut off;
in the Penglai Palace, the days and months are long.
Turning her head to look down on the human world,
she saw no Chang'an, only dust and mist.
Only with old things could she show her deep feeling:
the inlaid box and gold hairpin she sent along.
The hairpin she kept one strand, the box one half;
the hairpin split the gold, the box divided the inlay.
"If only our hearts are as firm as gold and inlay,
in heaven or among men we shall meet again."
At parting she earnestly gave a message once more,
in the message a vow that only their two hearts knew:
On the seventh day of the seventh month, in the Hall of Long Life,
at midnight, when no one was there and they spoke in private -
"In heaven, may we be birds that share one wing;
on earth, may we be branches that grow together."
Heaven lasts and earth endures, yet they have an end;
this sorrow goes on and on, with no end in time.

keyLines.line: 漢皇重色思傾國，御宇多年求不得。
keyLines.en: The Han emperor prized beauty and longed for a woman who could topple a state; for many years on the throne he sought one and could not find her.
keyLines.note: The opening uses 'the Han emperor' to stand for Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, a common way of speaking of one's own dynasty indirectly. It points out his love of beauty and so plants the seed of the whole tragedy.

keyLines.line: 迴眸一笑百媚生，六宮粉黛無顏色。
keyLines.en: One backward glance and a smile, and a hundred charms were born; the powdered and pencilled ladies of the six palaces lost their colour.
keyLines.note: It shows the charm of Yang Guifei once she had entered the palace: next to her, all the other women of the inner court seemed dull.

keyLines.line: 春宵苦短日高起，從此君王不早朝。
keyLines.en: The spring night is bitterly short, the sun is high when he rises; from then on the ruler does not hold early court.
keyLines.note: It hints that the emperor was sunk in pleasure and neglected the business of government. This is a foreshadowing of the An Lushan Rebellion.

keyLines.line: 六軍不發無奈何，宛轉娥眉馬前死。
keyLines.en: The six armies would not set out, and nothing could be done; with her curved moth brows, she died in front of the horses.
keyLines.note: The incident at Mawei Slope: as the court fled the rebels, the soldiers refused to go on, and forced the emperor to have Yang Guifei put to death.

keyLines.en: In the night rain, the sound of bells, a sound to break the heart.
