keyLines.note: On the emperor's flight to Shu, he heard bells in the night rain. The sound deepened his sorrow.

keyLines.line: 臨邛道士鴻都客，能以精誠致魂魄。
keyLines.en: A Daoist of Linqiong, a guest at Hongdu, could by utmost sincerity call back spirits.
keyLines.note: Here the poem turns to its second part: a master of occult arts goes through heaven and earth to find the consort's spirit.

keyLines.line: 玉容寂寞淚闌干，梨花一枝春帶雨。
keyLines.en: Her jade face is still and sad, her tears streaming; a spray of pear blossom, in spring, carrying rain.
keyLines.note: It describes the consort in the mountain of immortals. A face wet with tears like pear blossom in spring rain has become a classic comparison.

keyLines.line: 在天願作比翼鳥，在地願為連理枝。天長地久有時盡，此恨綿綿無絕期。
keyLines.en: In Heaven may we be birds that share one wing; on earth may we be branches that grow together. Heaven lasts and earth endures, yet they have an end; this sorrow goes on and on, with no end in time.
keyLines.note: The close of the whole poem. It recalls the vow on the Seventh Night at the Palace of Long Life, and states its theme: even Heaven and earth come to an end, but the sorrow does not.

glossary.note: A phrase for a woman of such beauty that a ruler might lose his kingdom for her.

glossary.en: Yu yang pi gu - 'the war drums of Yuyang'
glossary.note: Yuyang was in the area of present-day Ji county in Hebei, where An Lushan began his revolt. A pi gu is a military drum.
The armies of the emperor.
A place in present-day Xingping in Shaanxi, where Yang Guifei was made to die.
In ancient China, a man who claimed to seek immortality, make elixirs and communicate with spirits.
The Daoist name Yang Guifei took when she became a Daoist nun, before she entered the emperor's household.

glossary.en: dian he jin chai - 'inlaid box and gold hairpin'
glossary.note: A decorated box and a gold hairpin, which were love tokens.

glossary.en: bi yi niao, lian li zhi - 'birds with joined wings, branches grown together'
glossary.note: In legend, a bird that has only one wing and must fly joined with its mate, and two trees whose branches grow together. Both stand for a married couple deeply in love.

changhenge.background: Bai Juyi wrote this in 806, when he was a county defence officer at Zhouzhi. He and his friends Chen Hong and Wang Zhifu were visiting Xianyou Temple, and the talk turned to Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei. Chen Hong also wrote a prose story, the 'Tale of the Song of Everlasting Sorrow'.

pipaxing.summary: Bai Juyi's 'Song of the Pipa' is a long narrative poem written while he was in exile in Jiangzhou. At night by the Xunyang River, as he says goodbye to a guest, he hears a pipa. The woman player tells how she fell from fame to hardship. He feels the same sense of drifting, and in the last line, 'the Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue gown wet', he shows his tears of sympathy.
pipaxing.translation:
By the Xunyang River at night I was seeing off a guest;
maple leaves and reed blossoms, autumn rustling.
The host had dismounted, the guest was in the boat;
we raised wine to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Drunk without joy, we were sad to part;
at parting the river lay vast, steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly we heard a pipa over the water;
the host forgot to go home, the guest did not set out.
Following the sound, we quietly asked who was playing;
the pipa stopped, and she wanted to speak but was slow.
We moved our boat close and invited her to meet us,
added wine, turned the lamps, and began the feast again.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons she at last came out,
still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
Turning the pegs and plucking the strings, two or three notes -
before the tune had formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string muted and held back, each sound a thought,
as if telling of a whole life of disappointment.
With lowered brows, her hand free, she played on and on,
saying all the endless things in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly rubbing, then sweeping and plucking;
first "Rainbow Skirts", then "Green Waist".
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
the thin strings murmured like whispers.
Rumbling and murmuring, mixed and tangled as she played,
big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Warbling like an oriole's talk, gliding under the flowers;
sobbing like a spring, flowing hard beneath the ice.
The icy spring grew cold and rough, the strings seemed to freeze and break,
frozen and broken, no longer passing, the sound paused.
Another hidden sorrow and secret grief arose;
at that moment silence was better than sound.
Then a silver jug suddenly burst and the water spurted,
iron-clad horsemen charged out and blades and spears rang.
At the end of the tune she gathered her plectrum and swept it across the centre,
and the four strings gave one sound like tearing silk.
The boats east and the boats west were silent, without a word;
only the autumn moon was seen, white in mid-river.
Musing, she laid the plectrum down and tucked it between the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose and composed her face.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
whose home was below Toad Mound.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
and her name belonged to the first company of the Court Music Bureau.
When a tune ended, she made master musicians bow;
when she was made up, she was always envied by the other beauties.
The young men of the Five Mounds vied to give her head-wrap gifts;
for one tune, the red silk was past counting.
Her inlaid hairpin and cloud comb were broken beating the time;
her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
This year laughter and joy, and next year the same,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Her brother went off to the army, her aunt died;
evenings went and mornings came, and her looks faded.
Before her gate it grew cold and quiet, saddled horses few;
now grown old, she married and became a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left her at the river mouth to guard an empty boat;
around the boat the moon is bright and the river water cold.
Deep in the night she suddenly dreams of her youth,
and in the dream weeps, tears with her makeup running red.
I had sighed already at hearing the pipa,
and hearing these words I sighed again and again.
We are both people drifting at the edge of the sky;
why must we have known each other before we meet?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
and was sent down to live here, lying ill in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and there is no music,
all year I hear no sound of strings or pipes.
I live near the Pen River, on low, damp ground,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons' sad calls.
On spring river flower mornings, on autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Screeching and jabbering, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing you speak through the pipa,
it was like hearing immortal music, my ears brightened for a time.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more tune;
for you I will turn it into a "Song of the Pipa".
Moved by what I said, she stood a long while,
then sat back and tightened the strings, and the strings turned quick.
Bleak, bleak, not like the sound before;
everyone seated heard it again and hid their tears.
Who among those seated wept most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue gown wet.

keyLines.line: 潯陽江頭夜送客，楓葉荻花秋瑟瑟。
keyLines.en: By the Xunyang River at night I see off a guest; maple leaves and reed blossoms, autumn rustling.
keyLines.note: The opening sets the scene: a farewell at the riverside on an autumn night, in a bleak and chilly mood.

keyLines.line: 千呼萬喚始出來，猶抱琵琶半遮面。
keyLines.en: After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons she at last came out, still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
keyLines.note: This is the shy entrance of the pipa player, and a famous line for drawing a person.

keyLines.line: 轉軸撥絃三兩聲，未成曲調先有情。
keyLines.en: Turning the pegs and plucking the strings, two or three notes; before the tune has formed, the feeling is already there.
keyLines.note: Before the music even becomes a tune, feeling can be heard in it.

keyLines.line: 大絃嘈嘈如急雨，小絃切切如私語。嘈嘈切切錯雜彈，大珠小珠落玉盤。
keyLines.en: The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain, the thin strings murmured like whispers. Rumbling and murmuring mixed together, like big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
keyLines.note: The music is described through images: the heavy strings are like rain, the fine strings like private whispers, and the mixture is like pearls of different sizes dropping on a plate.

keyLines.line: 別有幽愁暗恨生，此時無聲勝有聲。
keyLines.en: Another hidden sorrow and secret grief arose; at that moment silence was better than sound.
keyLines.note: It describes a pause in the music, when the silence moves the listener more than the notes.

keyLines.line: 十三學得琵琶成，名屬教坊第一部。
keyLines.en: At thirteen I had learned the pipa to mastery; my name stood in the first company of the Court Music Bureau.
keyLines.note: The woman tells of her glory in the past, which sets up the contrast with her fall afterwards.

keyLines.line: 同是天涯淪落人，相逢何必曾相識。
keyLines.en: We are both people drifting at the edge of the sky; why must we have known each other before we meet?
keyLines.note: This is the emotional turn of the poem. The poet and the player find a bond in their shared downfall.

keyLines.line: 座中泣下誰最多，江州司馬青衫濕。
keyLines.en: Who among those seated wept most? The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue gown wet.
keyLines.note: In the ending, the poet says he is the one who wept most, until his blue gown was wet. The feeling lingers beyond the last line.

glossary.note: It can mean the sound of autumn wind, or a bluish-green colour. Here it means the bleak, rustling feeling of autumn.

glossary.en: Ni shang, Lu yao - 'Rainbow Skirts, Green Waist'
glossary.note: The names of two famous Tang tunes: the 'Rainbow Skirts and Feathered Robes' and the 'Green Waist'.
Words for sounds: cao cao for heavy, deep notes, qie qie for fine, broken ones.
The Tang office in charge of music and dance for the court.
Lengths of silk given as presents to singers and dancers. Later the term became a general word for rewards.
An assistant to the prefect of a prefecture. Bai Juyi was demoted to be the Sima of Jiangzhou, a post with little real power.
The colour of the robes worn by low-ranking officials in the Tang.
A tea-growing place in the Tang, in present-day Jingdezhen in Jiangxi.

pipaxing.background: In 815 Bai Juyi was demoted to Sima of Jiangzhou for speaking too frankly. In the autumn of 816 he was seeing off a guest at the Xunyang River, where he met the pipa player and wrote this poem. The poem has an original preface that explains the occasion.

dengyoujoutai.summary: A short ancient-style poem of uneven line lengths. Chen Zi'ang climbs Youzhou Terrace, and sees neither the men of the past nor those of the future. Facing the endless stretch of Heaven and earth, he weeps. The poem expresses the sorrow of an unrecognised talent and of loneliness.
dengyoujoutai.translation:
Ahead, I do not see the men of old;
Behind, I do not see those who will come.
Thinking of Heaven and earth, so boundless and enduring,
I am alone in my grief, and my tears fall.

glossary.note: Also called the Golden Terrace, said to have been built by King Zhao of Yan (4th-3rd century BC) to attract talented men. It lay near present-day Beijing.
Wise rulers of the past, such as King Zhao of Yan, who honoured able men.
Wise and able men of the future.
A mournful state of mind.
It describes something that goes on far and long, without end.

dengyoujoutai.background: Chen Zi'ang joined a military campaign against the Khitan around 696, in the Tang reign of Empress Wu Zetian. His advice was not accepted, and he climbed Youzhou Terrace and wrote this poem. He called for a return to the plain, vigorous style of earlier poetry and so started a new current in Tang poetry.

bingchexing.summary: A ge xing in which Du Fu shows the misery of years of war and conscription under Emperor Xuanzong: the families weeping at the farewell, white bones across the land, fields gone to waste and heavy taxes. Through a dialogue between the poet and a marching soldier, he accuses the court of waging war without end.
bingchexing.translation:
Carts rumble, horses whinny, and the men marching off each have bow and arrows at their waists.
Fathers, mothers, wives and children run to see them off; the dust is so thick that Xianyang Bridge cannot be seen.
They tug at clothes, stamp their feet, block the road and weep, and the weeping goes straight up to the clouds.
A passer-by at the roadside asks the marching men; the men only say the levies come too often.
Some at fifteen were sent north to guard the river, and at forty they are sent west to farm the frontier lands.
When they left, the village headman wrapped their heads for them; they come back white-haired, only to be sent to the border again.
On the frontier the blood that has flowed makes a sea, yet the Martial Emperor's wish to extend the borders has not ended.
Have you not heard that in the two hundred prefectures of Han east of the mountains,
Thousands of villages and tens of thousands of hamlets grow brambles and thorns?
Even if sturdy women take up hoe and plough, the crops grow in the fields with no order of east or west.
And the soldiers of Qin can endure hard fighting; they are driven like dogs and chickens.
Though an elder asks, how would a conscript dare to voice his bitterness?
Take this winter: the troops of Guanxi have still not been allowed to rest.
The county officials press hard for the rent; where will the taxes come from?
I now truly know that bearing sons is bad, and that bearing daughters is better.
A daughter can still be married to a neighbour; a son is buried and lost among the hundred weeds.
Have you not seen, by the shore of Qinghai, white bones from ancient times that no one gathers?
New ghosts, wronged and troubled, and old ghosts weep; on dark days and in wet rain their voices whimper and wail.

glossary.note: The sound of cartwheels.
The sound of horses neighing.
A bridge over the Wei River north-west of Chang'an, on the main road west for troops going to the front.

glossary.en: dian xing - 'calling up by the roll'
glossary.note: Conscripting soldiers by going down the household registers.
A low-level local official in the Tang who kept the household registers and organised taxes and labour service.
Emperor Wu of Han, who fought long wars on the frontiers. Du Fu uses him as a cover for Emperor Xuanzong of Tang.
The lands east of Mount Hua.

glossary.en: Qing hai tou - 'the shore of Qinghai'
glossary.note: The area around Qinghai Lake, where Tang forces fought the Tibetans.

bingchexing.background: Du Fu wrote this around 751. The Tang was then fighting year after year against Nanzhao in the south-west and the Tibetans in the west, with great numbers of men called up. The poem uses Emperor Wu of Han as a stand-in for Xuanzong. It is a famous example of Du Fu's 'new yuefu', in which he made up his own titles for poems about events of his day.
